title: Happy Eyeballs Version 2: Better Connectivity Using Concurrency
summary: Hostnames often resolve to several IP addresses, and some addresses or address families may be broken or slow. Happy Eyeballs version 2 lets clients try multiple connections concurrently, with short delays, so users get a working, fast connection quickly. It updates the idea from the original specification.

plainLanguage.summary: If two doors might be locked, you try one, and if it is slow, try the other soon after. You use whichever opens first.

questions: how to choose between ipv4 and ipv6 quickly
what is the happy eyeballs resolution delay
what is the connection attempt delay in happy eyeballs
subtitle: Race connection attempts to IPv6 and IPv4 addresses with short delays so users get a working connection fast.

tldr.problem: A hostname often resolves to several addresses, and some addresses or address families may be blocked, broken or slow, so a client that tries them one at a time can leave users waiting.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends AAAA and A queries asynchronously, sorts the resulting addresses, interleaves address families and starts connection attempts one after another with short delays, keeping the first to succeed.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes the original algorithm description in RFC 6555 and adds DNS handling, multi-address lists, historical data and support for IPv6-only networks with NAT64 and DNS64.

today: RFC 8305 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 6555. The metadata for this unit lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Many protocols use hostnames, and a hostname often resolves to multiple IP addresses with different performance and connectivity. Specific addresses or address families (IPv4 or IPv6) may be blocked, broken or sub-optimal on a network, so a client that attempts several connections in parallel has a chance of connecting more quickly.

RFC 8305 specifies requirements for algorithms that reduce this user-visible delay and gives an example algorithm called Happy Eyeballs, a technique for dual-stack hosts. It obsoletes the original description in RFC 6555, refined now that the approach has been deployed at scale and measured for several years, in the RFC's words. It assumes a host preference for IPv6 over IPv4 and says the recommendations are easy to adapt if the host prefers otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: When a website has more than one way to reach it, some ways may be broken. Happy Eyeballs quietly tries more than one so you do not sit waiting on a broken one.

sections.title: The Four Phases
sections.content:
The "Happy Eyeballs Connection Setup" has four phases: start asynchronous DNS queries, sort the resolved destination addresses, start asynchronous connection attempts, and establish one connection, which cancels all other attempts.

The goal is to avoid delaying the user whenever possible while still preferring IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask for the addresses, put them in a sensible order, try them one by one with short pauses, and stop as soon as one works.

sections.title: Handling DNS Queries
sections.content:
A client with both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity sends both an AAAA query and an A query as close together as possible, AAAA first. It SHOULD NOT wait for both answers: DNS resolution should be asynchronous, and if the platform has no asynchronous DNS API the behaviour can be simulated with two synchronous queries on different threads.

If a positive AAAA answer arrives first, the first IPv6 attempt starts immediately. If a positive A answer arrives first, the client SHOULD wait a short Resolution Delay, recommended at 50 milliseconds, for the AAAA answer so IPv6 keeps its preference. If no usable AAAA answer arrives by then, the client moves on with the IPv4 addresses it has. If the AAAA answer shows up later but before any connection is established, its addresses join the candidate list.

For DNS servers themselves, queries SHOULD go over IPv6 first; an IPv6 server address that gets no response may be marked penalized. Clients SHOULD NOT impose an explicit limit on the number of configured DNS servers, and if hardware forces one they SHOULD keep at least one address from each family.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask two questions at once, "what is its newer address?" and "what is its older address?". If the older answer comes back first, you wait a tiny moment to see if the newer one follows.

sections.title: Sorting Addresses
sections.content:
Before connecting, the client orders the addresses it has from both families. It MUST first sort them using Destination Address Selection from RFC 6724. A stateful client with round-trip time history SHOULD add a rule between rules 8 and 9 preferring lower RTTs, and a client that tracks past use SHOULD add another rule preferring addresses it used before. That helps servers that use the client address during authentication, as with TCP Fast Open and some HTTP cookies. Such history MUST NOT be used across different network interfaces and SHOULD be flushed when the device changes network.

The client SHOULD then interleave the families: if the first address is IPv6, the first IPv4 address moves to second place. An implementation MAY favour a family by trying more than one of its addresses first; that number is the First Address Family Count. Interleaving avoids waiting through a long list of one family when it is impaired. Source address selection is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: You line up the doors, taking turns between the two kinds, so one broken kind cannot hold you up for long.

sections.title: Staggered Connection Attempts
sections.content:
To avoid unreasonable network load, connection attempts SHOULD NOT start all at once. One attempt starts first, then the others one at a time, and earlier attempts keep running. When one attempt succeeds, generally when the TCP handshake completes, all others SHOULD be cancelled and untried addresses ignored. The resolver SHOULD still process DNS replies for a short time, recommended at 1 second, to fill the cache.

The wait between attempts is the Connection Attempt Delay, with a recommended default of 250 milliseconds. A more nuanced client can aim for the moment the previous attempt sends its second TCP SYN, using the retransmission timer from RFC 6298. The delay MUST have a lower bound: a new attempt MUST NOT start within 10 milliseconds of the previous one, and the recommended Minimum Connection Attempt Delay is 100 milliseconds, to avoid congestion collapse under high packet loss. It SHOULD have an upper bound, with a recommended Maximum Connection Attempt Delay of 2 seconds.

If DNS answers change during setup, an address removed after its attempt started is left to continue, one removed before is dropped from the list, and an added address is sorted into the not-yet-attempted addresses by the rules above.
sections.plainLanguage: You try the first door, and if it has not opened after a short wait you try the second while still pushing on the first. The moment one opens, you stop trying the rest.

sections.title: IPv6-Only Networks with NAT64 and DNS64
sections.content:
On IPv6-only networks using NAT64 and DNS64, a Happy Eyeballs engine on platforms without 464XLAT SHOULD follow section 7, and only when it detects such a network. A simple heuristic is routable IPv6, no routable IPv4 and a DNS resolver address.

  • IPv4 literals: the engine queries the network for the NAT64 prefix (RFC 7050), synthesizes IPv6 addresses (RFC 6052) and inserts them into the list as if they came from DNS.
  • Broken AAAA records: for hostnames with an A record and an AAAA record that never answers, DNS64 cannot synthesize addresses. After a Last Resort Local Synthesis Delay, recommended at 2 seconds from the last attempt, the client queries the A record and synthesizes locally.
  • VPNs: a VPN resolver may return an IPv4-only answer the underlying network cannot reach, so the client resolves the A record with that resolver and synthesizes an IPv6 address locally.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks only speak the new address style. The device has to translate old-style addresses itself, like using a phrasebook when the local language is different.

sections.title: Defaults, Limits and Security
sections.content:
Section 8 lists the configurable values and recommended defaults: Resolution Delay 50 ms, First Address Family Count 1 (2 may be used to favour a family more), Connection Attempt Delay 250 ms, Minimum Connection Attempt Delay 100 ms (never under 10 ms), Maximum Connection Attempt Delay 2 seconds and Last Resort Local Synthesis Delay 2 seconds. The RFC says they were determined empirically from timing on a wide set of production devices, may change over time, and that implementors may use different values without changing the specification.

Limitations: Happy Eyeballs only acts at the initial handshake, so MTU problems can go unnoticed, and it cannot tell if an application on a chosen server, such as TLS or HTTP, works. It can also hide operational issues, for example an IPv6 failure masked by working IPv4, so operators are advised to monitor all address families externally.

For security, applications should not rely on a stable hostname-to-address mapping, and Happy Eyeballs may make it more likely that later connections to one hostname use different IP addresses. There are no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The waiting times are sensible guesses from real measurements. Because the trick hides broken doors from visitors, the people who run the building should still check every door.
